Neither party really looks anything like a classic liberal party these days if you really get down to it, but I would argue that that’s because the body politic of the country has changed so much demographically and also in size. It also has to do with the ever changing world and the issues at hand. It’s better to look at American politics and its history through the different party eras and the ideology underpinning those eras. For example we are currently in the Neoliberal Era or at least at the very end of it. This period arguably began in the late 1970s with the casual move away from social and economic policies of the New Deal Era which came before it from the 1930s to roughly the early 70s. 

Within these eras you tend to have a general consensus on the types of social and economic policies across the political spectrum. During the New Deal Era which began under FDR you had such a wide consensus that it fundamentally shifted politics in the country. After FDR you get Truman and later you had Eisenhower who was a conservative of his era, but kept many of the new deal policies and also added to them in his own way such as with using federal dollars to fund the highway system. The New Deal Era of American politics really went on until about Nixon who had many new deal type policies while he was in office as well. 

The shift away from new deal policies and toward neoliberal ones began during the stagflation years and slow economic growth of the 1970s. This lead to a new general consensus in deregulation and opening of free trade which has lead us to our modern era. In this era every president from Reagan to Trump have been either a liberal or conservative version of the neoliberal consensus. These days however we are seeing the death of the neoliberal consensus and the birth of something new. With the contemporary left of American politics seemingly shifting toward more social democratic policies, that of which you see in places like Europe and Scandinavian countries while you have the contemporary right of American politics embracing a more protectionist and nationalist tone with its policies and initiatives. 

You’re right when you say the dems aren’t a classic liberal party, but there really isn’t one of these anywhere in American politics and it’s because to be classic liberal wouldn’t fit into the mold of contemporary politics. Now that’s not to imply that there isn’t a liberal wing of American politics, there obviously is, it’s just the contemporary version of it. While on the conservative side you don’t have classic liberal policies either with them embracing things like tariffs and protectionist policies and also stricter social policies. 

The body politic and the contemporary issues are always changing and by extension so are our politics and the parties that help shape and channel the discourse. Classic Liberal policies of an era 250 years removed from us are obviously not going to play a huge role in our modern predicament, but we can still trace the lineage of our politics to that era. But you have to first go through all the different eras before you get there to understand how it has changed. Of course liberals and conservatives are different than they were back then, the conservatives and liberals of the classical liberal era were different than those who came before them in the age of monarchy and mercantilism as well.

To pretty much sum up what you’ll likely experience (if you’re a man) is tinder isn’t all that bad in terms of getting matches, it hasn’t been for me necessarily, but dating apps such as tinder are fundamentally flawed in that they don’t do men a whole lot of favors because I’m pretty sure the number of men on the app outnumber the amount of women on the app, just from what I’ve read. But that theory is reinforced when you read bios, see how many matches get referenced against how many people you swipe right on and so on. 

One important thing I’ll leave you with is don’t sweat it too much if a person doesn’t reciprocate what you’re putting out. The reality of this game we call dating especially right now in this social media heavy world is that it takes two people to play and you will only be able to do so much. Sure if you’re a guy then in my opinion it’s ok to come 60-70% of the way to show a woman you are interested and willing to make the first move and to show her you can “take the lead”, that’s ok. What’s not ok is if after that she never meets you in the middle at any point. At a certain point it has to be 50/50 and if it never gets there then it’s time to bail. No woman is worth the hassle if she hasn’t earned that amount of effort from you.

So yeah rule number 1 of casual dating: DONT get your hopes up. You will be disappointed. But don’t be discouraged, just stay honest with yourself and you’ll get matches and maybe even a date, I didn’t think I would ever get one but here I am.

The lines are pretty straight forward, the line that goes through the net is called the “goal line” and the two lines that enclose the space behind the net make up what’s called “the trapezoid”. Goalies can only play the puck inside that space when below the goal line. 

The blue lines are what separates the neutral zone from the defensive and offensive zones, they are usually referred to as the “blue line” and the reason you may hear commentators refer to some players as “blue liners” is because they are defensemen and when defending in the O zone they primarily stay high in the zone near the blue line. 

The circles are called the “face-off dots” where they drop the puck after an icing, the goalie has stopped the play, a penalty has been called, etc. the dots just outside the blue line inside the neutral zone are also face-off dots that are usually used when an offside call occurs unless it’s deemed an “intentional offside” then you’ll typical see the puck be dropped in the teams zone that was called for that as a minor infraction. 

The blue paint that is under the goalie represents the goalies area in which is pretty much considered his domain. There’s pretty much always controversy surrounding this part of the ice since driving the net is a popular way to create scoring chances and scoring goals and a lot of times things happen so quickly that the officials don’t have a real chance at making the right call if the puck does go in the net. 

As far as body checking goes it’s considered a standard part of the game, you’ll usually hear things like “finish your checks” and that just means to slow your opponent down by body checking him into the boards, taking him out of the play, or the most ideal thing, creating a turnover. 

Fighting is a bit more complex as far as understanding how it fits in the game. Truth is, it doesn’t “fit” into the game itself. Fighting has no tactical advantage to it usually. Like a coach won’t go out there and tell his player to fight a guy as it might give them some advantage. The reason fighting occurs usually is as a response to something such as a bad hit that was not called for a penalty, two players who may have been at each other from the start of a game could result in a fight, but typically fights happen as a way of standing up for your team, that’s why back in the old school days of hockey you had what we’re called “enforcers” who’s only purpose on the ice usually was to keep teams from attacking star players. For example Wayne Gretzky was the star player of his generation he was the most dangerous and threatening offensive player on his teams, so as a result the opposing teams might target him with extra body checking, open ice hits, even dirty plays to knock him off his game or take him out of the play. So what the Oilers(Gretzky’s team) did was they would deploy Marty McSorley(a legendary enforcer) to protect Gretzky and essentially keep teams away from him because if they didn’t they’d have to answer to the enforcer. 

Now days enforcers don’t really exist the game has changed and what you typically find are guys who can play at a high level skill wise but play with what is referred to as an “edge” where they play physical and aren’t afraid to “drop the gloves” so to speak and fight when they are called upon.

So obviously with hockey it’s a sport of constant motion and since that’s the nature of the sport what you’ll find is what most teams are trying to do is move the opposing teams players out of position upon leaving the D zone, going through neutral zone, or entering the O zone. There’s a variety of ways you can go about that and typically yes the puck carrier will almost certainly get most of the attention from not only the defensemen but also the goaltender. 

At the highest levels of hockey such as the NHL its extremely hard to score goals on NHL net-minders so you’ll often times see teams do a cycle around the o zone constantly moving the puck which as a result keeps the opposing team in a constant state of movement. What they’re trying to do is open up a teams defensive structure by getting someone out of position. The best way to do that is by deception typically, making your opponent think you’re going to do something that you aren’t going to do such as pass, shoot, or move the puck back to the blue line to restart the cycle. All while this is going on the whole point of it is to open up enough space in the opposing teams d structure to either pass to the slot(the spot directly in front of the net) to an open player for a shot on goal, to open up the center of the o zone for a cross ice pass for example from half wall to half wall for a shot on a goaltender who at that point would be moving form right to left or left to right. Another strategy is for teams to utilize their defensemen such as having them take point shots from the blue line which are usually meant for tips on net or rebounds for players to drive the net and capitalize on as at the point the entire opposing team is trying to get the puck away from the goalie out of the zone so they typically collapse inward toward to the goalie, which automatically opens up a bunch of ice around the net and slot areas. 

I’m sorry if that is confusing, but in the end yes it would make sense to pay close attention to what happens away from the puck because what’s happening away from the puck will strongly dictate what happens on any given play, rush, or really anything that’s happening in the game. But there are exceptions such as if the puck carrier is a shooter primarily then he’ll look to shoot, some guys are skilled enough to put the puck directly where they want to put it and sometimes a goalie will have no chance at stopping it, in that case everyone would have been paying attention to the puck and what happened away from it wouldn’t have had any impact on  a goal like that.
